title: “Stand and Practice? What Kind of PD is That?”
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart describes attending a Character Lab workshop led by researcher Chris Hulleman, where participants paired up and stood to rehearse delivering instructions, then trade feedback. He connects this to teacher Lynsay Fabio's school, where stand-and-practice is a routine part of PD, and to Doug Lemov and colleagues' Practice Perfect, which argues that workshops fail when teachers must learn new techniques in the live match. The central claim is that teaching is a physical performance skill, so improvement in things like clear directions or calm correction comes through repeated rehearsal before students are present. His advice is twofold: leaders should build on-your-feet practice into PD sessions, and individual teachers should rehearse a technique right after reading about it. The ending promotes an associated course, but the argument about practice-based PD stands on its own.
points: Hulleman's workshop modeled PD as practice, with partners simulating the intervention in timed rounds and giving feedback.
Lynsay Fabio argues teaching is physical as well as intellectual, so skills like giving instructions must be rehearsed aloud before class.
Practice Perfect's tennis analogy diagnoses why telling-style workshops fail: teachers end up learning a new backhand mid-match.
Stuart's recommendations are concrete: leaders embed rehearsal in PD, and teachers stand and practice a new idea immediately instead of waiting for game time.
quotes: But Chris had an interesting bent toward leading professional development. Instead of just telling us about the intervention and giving us bits of time periodically in which to discuss it, he actually had us doing on odd thing.

Listening partner, your job will be to make 1-2 notes for feedback after the speaking partner is through with the simulation. After three minutes, we’ll sound a chime, and it’ll be time to switch roles.
Professional development as practice. That’s what Chris was doing. And amazingly, it was a semi-novel idea to me.

Sometimes we get stuck thinking of teaching as just an intellectual effort, but it’s hugely physical, too,” Lynsay explained. “So, if our goal is to get better at delivering clear instructions, say, or correcting misbehavior with emotional constancy, then these are things we’ve got to stand up and do, repeatedly, before we’re with students.

We realized that our workshop participants, on returning to their classrooms, were trying to do the equivalent of walking onto center court at Wimbledon and learning a new style of backhand in the midst of a match,” the authors write. “We realized… that we would have to approach teaching like tennis” (7).

For leaders, it seems to me that we must find opportunities to incorporate on-your-feet practice into our professional development sessions — just as Dr. Hulleman did at the workshop I attended. And for teachers, the next time you read something in a book or a blog post that you’d like to try, don’t wait until game time — stand up and practice it right then and there.
